stages.name: Plan & select
qs: Which of our data and systems will you access — and from which countries?
Do you hold ISO/IEC 27001, a SOC 2 Type II report or a national scheme such as BSI C5, SecNumCloud or ENS?
Will you use our data to train AI models — and can we opt out in the contract?
Who are your sub-processors and fourth parties?
How do you build securely — SBOM, signed releases, a vulnerability disclosure policy?

stages.name: Contract
qs: Will you notify us of incidents within [X] hours — shorter than our own deadline (NIS2 24 h; DORA 4 h after classification)?
Will you give us audit rights and cooperate with our regulators?
Will you commit to where our data is stored — and to returning it and certifying its deletion at exit?
Will you agree security requirements, patch timelines and coordinated vulnerability disclosure?
Will you give notice — and seek our approval — before changing sub-processors?

stages.name: Onboard
qs: Who are your 24/7 security and incident contacts — and can we test them?
Will every account you use with us have MFA and only the access it needs?
Will you connect only through managed, logged channels?
Can you give us what we need for our asset, data-flow and register-of-information records?

stages.name: Operate & monitor
qs: Will you share fresh evidence every year — certificates, pen-test summaries, policies?
Can we review your accounts and access to our systems every quarter?
How will you tell us about advisories, breaches and known-exploited vulnerabilities in your products?
Will you run a joint exercise with us at least once a year?

stages.name: Incident
qs: What happened, when — and is it contained?
Is our data or service affected — and which indicators should we block?
Which authorities have you notified, and when?
Who speaks to the press — and can we agree messages before anything is published?

stages.name: Exit
qs: How and when will you return our data — and certify its deletion?
Will you revoke every account, key and connection on the last day?
How will you support the transition to a new provider?
Will you keep the logs we need for investigations and audits — and for how long?

laws.name: NIS2
laws.who: Essential and important entities in 18 sectors, including managed (security) service providers.
laws.duty: Supply-chain security (Art. 21(2)(d)); weigh each direct supplier’s vulnerabilities and secure-development practices (Art. 21(3)). Management bodies approve and oversee measures (Art. 20).
laws.clock: Early warning 24 h · notification 72 h · final report 1 month (Art. 23)

laws.name: DORA
laws.who: Financial entities — and EU oversight of critical ICT third-party providers.
laws.duty: ICT third-party risk and a register of information (Art. 28); key contract provisions including incident help, audit and exit (Art. 30); resilience testing (Art. 24–26).
laws.clock: Initial 4 h after classifying as major (≤ 24 h after detection) · intermediate 72 h · final 1 month

laws.name: GDPR
laws.who: Anyone processing personal data — controllers and their processors.
laws.duty: Processor contracts and approval of sub-processors (Art. 28).
laws.clock: Processor → controller without undue delay (Art. 33(2)) · controller → authority within 72 h (Art. 33(1)) · tell people if high risk (Art. 34)

laws.name: Cyber Resilience Act
laws.who: Manufacturers of products with digital elements sold in the EU.
laws.duty: Security by design, vulnerability handling and a software bill of materials for products.
laws.clock: Actively exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents: early warning within 24 h, from 11 September 2026

laws.name: EU AI Act
laws.who: Providers and deployers of AI systems, and providers of general-purpose AI models.
laws.duty: Responsibilities along the AI value chain (Art. 25); GPAI providers give documentation to downstream providers (Art. 53); deployers monitor and inform providers (Art. 26).
laws.clock: Providers report serious incidents of high-risk AI (Art. 73) — within 15 days, faster in the most critical cases

clock.title: Supplier detects
clock.text: They notify you as the contract requires; as a processor they must tell you without undue delay.

clock.title: You triage
clock.text: Which services, data and connections are affected? Activate your incident team and cut risky links.

clock.title: DORA initial
clock.text: Financial entities: initial notification within 4 hours of classifying a major ICT incident.

clock.title: NIS2 early warning
clock.text: Send it to your CSIRT or authority if the incident is significant for you — even with partial facts.

clock.title: Notify in full
clock.text: NIS2 incident notification, GDPR breach notification and DORA intermediate report.

clock.title: Final reports
clock.text: NIS2 and DORA final reports. Lessons learnt, contract fixes and a supplier reassessment.

examples.text: Ransomware at a check-in software supplier disrupted Brussels, Berlin and Heathrow.
A file-transfer zero-day exposed staff data at organisations that never ran MOVEit themselves.
One municipal IT provider’s ransomware attack stopped citizen services across a German region.
Stolen passwords on cloud accounts without MFA led to data theft at many customers.

contacts.dpa: State data-protection authority (BfDI for federal bodies)

contacts.crime: Police or gendarmerie; cybermalveillance.gouv.fr for help

contacts.dpa: Garante per la protezione dei dati personali

tests.title: Run a joint tabletop every year
tests.text: Invite your top suppliers; use a real case such as MOVEit or Collins Aerospace.

tests.title: Test the contact tree
tests.text: Call each supplier’s 24/7 line out of hours (announced) and log the response time.

tests.title: Check the clocks
tests.text: Do contractual notification times beat your NIS2, DORA and GDPR deadlines?

tests.title: Pre-fill the regulator templates
tests.text: NIS2 early warning, DORA initial notification and GDPR breach forms — ready before you need them.

tests.title: Follow DORA testing duties
tests.text: A digital operational resilience testing programme (Art. 24–25); threat-led penetration testing at least every three years for designated entities (Art. 26).

tests.title: Measure effectiveness
tests.text: NIS2 Art. 21(2)(f) asks for policies to assess whether your measures work. Exercises are your evidence.

injects.text: Your payroll provider emails: ‘suspicious activity — investigating’.
A ransomware group lists your company on its leak site, naming the supplier.
A journalist calls. The supplier still can’t say what data was taken.
Your NIS2 early warning is due in four hours. The facts are still unclear.

discuss: Do we report with partial facts? (The early warning is meant to be early.)
Is this a personal-data breach — and whose 72 hours are running?
Do we suspend the integration, and what stops working?
Who briefs staff whose bank details may be exposed?
